claim: The basal ganglia are involved in the planning, execution and control of gripping force and movement vigour.
source: The basal ganglia are known to be involved in the planning, execution and control of gripping force and movement vigour.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: STN LFP activities in the gamma (55–90 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) bands are most informative about gripping force.
source: We found that STN LFP activities in the gamma (55–90 Hz) and beta (13–30m Hz) bands were most informative about gripping force
evidence: This finding is based on the experimental data and model comparisons presented in the study.

claim: A first order dynamic linear model with STN LFP features as inputs can decode the temporal profile of gripping force.
source: a first order dynamic linear model with these STN LFP features as inputs can be used to decode the temporal profile of gripping force
evidence: This is demonstrated through the experimental results and model validation presented in the study.

claim: Deep brain LFPs could potentially be used to decode movement parameters related to force and movement vigour for the development of advanced human-machine interfaces.
source: deep brain LFPs could potentially be used to decode movement parameters related to force and movement vigour for the development of advanced human-machine interfaces
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications based on the study's findings.

claim: No BMI user has yet achieved manipulation of the force generated by a robotic hand.
source: no BMI user has yet achieved manipulation of the force generated by a robotic hand (Velliste et al., 2008; Collinger et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Motor areas of the basal ganglia have been associated with the scaling of motor vigour.
source: Motor areas of the basal ganglia have long been associated with the scaling of motor vigour, measured in terms of the amplitude and speed of a movement or gripping force, although this is certainly not likely to be their exclusive function (DeLong and Wichmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neuronal recordings in monkeys and imaging studies in healthy humans have suggested that the basal ganglia play an important role in the control of the scaling of motor responses.
source: Neuronal recordings in monkeys and imaging studies in healthy humans have suggested that the basal ganglia play an important role in the control of the scaling of motor responses (DeLong et al., 1984; Turner and Anderson, 1997; Spraker et al., 2007; Vaillancourt et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The power over the gamma band (60–80 Hz) in the LFP in the globus pallidus correlates with the movement amplitude and velocity of the contralateral hand of patients with cranial dystonia.
source: the power over the gamma band (60–80 Hz) in the LFP in the globus pallidus correlates with the movement amplitude and velocity of the contralateral hand of patients with cranial dystonia (Brücke et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In patients with Parkinson's disease, movement speed correlates with the power in the gamma band in the LFP from the STN.
source: Similar correlations have been noted in patients with Parkinson's disease between movement speed and the power in the gamma band in the LFP picked up from the STN (Joundi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Suppression in the beta band (13–30 Hz) and power increase in the gamma band of the STN LFP may correlate with forces or efforts made over the lower and higher effort ranges, respectively.
source: Our previous studies also showed that suppression in the beta band (13–30 Hz) and power increase in the gamma band of the STN LFP may correlate with forces or efforts made over the lower and higher effort ranges, respectively, in a manner independent from the effector that was activated (Tan et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: A significant reduction of power in the beta band (13–30 Hz) and increase in power in the broad gamma band (55–90 Hz) was observed during gripping in one group of electrodes (n = 9).
source: From one group of electrodes (n = 9), a significant reduction of power in the beta band (13–30 Hz) and increase in power in the broad gamma band (55–90 Hz) was observed during gripping.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In another group of electrodes (n = 9), significant simultaneous modulation was absent in the beta and gamma band with movement.
source: In another group of electrodes (n = 9), significant simultaneous modulation was absent in the beta and gamma band with movement, and there was instead an increased power across the low frequency band during gripping.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In group 1, the stable force during the holding phase and the peak force yank in the force initialisation phase scaled well with self-rated effort (SRE).
source: Trajectories of force (D) and force yank (G) for Group one show that the stable force during the holding phase (1–2 s after cue) as well as the peak force yank in the force initialisation phase scaled well with self-rated effort (SRE).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and G.

claim: Group 2 had significantly lower correlation coefficients between stable force and SRE compared with group 1 (p<0.0001).
source: Group two had significantly lower correlation coefficients between stable force and SRE (F) and between the peak force yank and SRE (I) compared with group 1 (p<0.0001)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 1F and I.

claim: The Spearman correlation coefficient between stable force and SRE in group 1 ranged between 0.6454 and 0.9728 (median value = 0.9409).
source: The Spearman correlation coefficient between stable force and SRE ranged between 0.6454 and 0.9728 (median value = 0.9409, Figure 1F)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The correlation coefficient between peak force yank and SRE in group 1 ranged between 0.4514 and 0.9341 (median value = 0.8688).
source: the correlation coefficient between peak force yank and SRE ranged between 0.4514 and 0.9341 (median value = 0.8688, Figure 1I)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the stable force and self-rated effort in group 2 ranged between 0.0258 and 0.8334 (median value = 0.6023).
source: The correlation coefficient between the stable force and self-rated effort in the second group (ranged between 0.0258 and 0.8334, median value = 0.6023) was significantly lower than in the first group (t(16)=5.386, p<0.0001 with un-paired t-test applied to Fisher transformed r values, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the peak force yank and SRE in group 2 ranged between −0.4992 and 0.6944 (median value = 0.3791).
source: The correlation coefficient between the peak force yank and SRE in the second group (ranged between −0.4992 and 0.6944, median value = 0.3791) was also significantly lower (t(16)=4.977, p=0.0001 with un-paired t-test applied to Fisher transformed r values).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Patients in group 2 exhibited impairment in the scaling of force with effort.
source: Thus, patients in the second group exhibited impairment in the scaling of force with effort.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data comparing the two groups.

claim: The lack of beta and gamma reactivity during gripping in group 2 would be consistent with a role for these activities in the coding of effort into force.
source: The lack of beta and gamma reactivity during gripping in this group would be consistent with a role for these activities in the coding of effort in to force.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed LFP patterns with functional implications.

claim: Movement-related modulations in beta and gamma bands were presumed to indicate recordings made in or near the dorsal STN.
source: (2) movement-related modulations were presumed to indicate recordings made in or near the dorsal STN
evidence: This is an assumption made by the researchers based on known neurophysiology.

claim: Significant movement-related modulations were taken as evidence of relatively physiological functioning given that the motor reactivity of the two rhythms is increased by dopaminergic medication.
source: significant movement-related modulations were taken as evidence of relatively physiological functioning given that the motor reactivity of the two rhythms is increased by dopaminergic medication (Anzak et al., 2012)
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Lack of movement related modulations might indicate a temporary surgical stun effect and temporary damage to the STN or targeting variance.
source: lack of movement related modulations might indicate a temporary surgical stun effect and temporary damage to the STN (Chen et al., 2006) or targeting variance
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Model 2 was significantly better than Models 4–8 in terms of BIC after FDR multiple comparison correction.
source: Paired t-tests showed that Model 2 was significantly better, in terms of BIC, than Models 4–8 after FDR multiple comparison correction: (t(8)=−3.63, p=0.007 compared with Model 4; t(8)=−4.950, p=0.001 compared with Model 5; t(8)=−9.347, p<0.001 compared with Model 6; t(8)=−5.757, p<0.001 compared with Model 7; t(8)=−3.675, p=0.007 compared with Model 8).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model comparison analysis.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the predicted force and the measured force across all STNs was between 0.902 and 0.987 with a median value of 0.952 for high effort force.
source: The correlation coefficient between the predicted force and the measured force across all STNs was between 0.902 and 0.987 with a median value of 0.952 for high effort force (data during low effort used for model parameter estimation)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the force prediction analysis.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the predicted force and the measured force was between 0.921 and 0.992 with a median value of 0.969 for low effort force.
source: between 0.921 and 0.992 with a median value of 0.969 for low effort force (data during high effort used for model parameter estimation)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the force prediction analysis.

claim: The nRMSE of the prediction force was between 5.60% and 28.07% with median value of 16.5% for high effort levels.
source: The nRMSE of the prediction force was between 5.60% and 28.07% with median value of 16.5% for high effort levels
evidence: This is a quantitative result measuring prediction accuracy.

claim: The nRMSE of the prediction force was between 10.5% and 23.8% with median value of 16.4% for low effort levels.
source: between 10.5% and 23.8% with median value of 16.4% for low effort levels
evidence: This is a quantitative result measuring prediction accuracy.

claim: The differences in reaction times between the predicted force and the measured force were not significantly different from zero for both high and low effort levels.
source: The differences in reaction times (DifRT) between the predicted force and the measured force were 11 ± 27 ms for high effort levels and −26 ± 31 ms for low effort levels. These were not significantly different from zero (t = 1.25, p=0.247 for high effort levels and t = 1.03, p=0.333 for low effort levels, one-sampled t-test compared to zero).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the timing analysis.

claim: For half of all the individual trials from one exemplar STN (n = 21), the within-trial correlation coefficient between the predicted force and measured force was equal or larger than 0.78.
source: For half of all the individual trials (n = 21) recorded from this STN and contralateral hand, the within-trial correlation coefficient between the predicted force and measured force was equal or larger than 0.78.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from individual trial analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The predicted stable force correlated with the measured stable force (n = 21, r = 0.815, p<0.001) for the exemplar STN.
source: This predicted stable force correlated with the measured stable force (n = 21, r = 0.815, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The regression gradient between predicted and measured stable force was close to unity (y = 0.96x + 2.4), suggesting no systematic overestimation or underestimation.
source: The line of best fit between the predicted stable force and measured stable force was y = 0.96x + 2.4. The regression gradient close to unity suggests that the prediction matches well with the measurement with no systematic overestimation or underestimation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from regression analysis with interpretation.

claim: Considering all the STNs with significant movement-related modulations in both beta and gamma bands (N = 9), the correlation between the predicted stable force and measured stable force across trials ranged from 0.448 to 0.913 for the contralateral hand when Model 2 was used.
source: Considering all the STNs in which significant movement-related modulations were observed in both beta and gamma bands (N = 9), the correlation between the predicted stable force and measured stable force across trials ranged from 0.448 to 0.913 for the contralateral hand when Model 2 was used
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis across multiple STNs.

claim: The regression gradient between the predicted stable force and measured stable force ranged from 0.91 to 1.12 and was not significantly different from unity across STNs (p=0.431).
source: with the regression gradient between the predicted stable force and measured stable force ranging from 0.91 to 1.12 (not significantly different from unity across STNs based on one-sampled T-test, p=0.431)
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis.

claim: The median value for the within-trial correlation coefficient was 0.732 for Model 2 considering all individual trials from the 9 STNr.
source: Considering all the individual trials from the 9 STNr, the median value for the within-trial correlation coefficient was 0.732 for Model 2 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 5.

claim: Around 13% of trials had negative correlation between the measured force and the predicted force, suggesting a failure in predicting force trajectory.
source: There were around 13% of trials during which the correlation between the measured force and the predicted force were negative, suggesting a failure in predicting force trajectory.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data with interpretation.

claim: The cross-trial correlations between the predicted stable force and measured stable force were significantly lower for the ipsilateral hand than for the contralateral hand (F(2,16)=10.629, p=0.012).
source: The cross-trial correlations between the predicted stable force and measured stable were significantly lower for the ipsilateral hand than for the contralateral hand (F(2,16)=10.629, p=0.012).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing laterality of force prediction.

claim: The distributions of WithinR for ipsilateral force prediction were significantly different from that for the contralateral force prediction (ks-test p<0.001).
source: The distributions of WithinR for ipsilateral force prediction were significantly different from that for the contralateral force prediction (ks-test p<0.001 no matter whether Model 1, Model 2 or Model 3 was used)
evidence: This is a statistical result from distribution comparison.

claim: The STNr LFP was more informative in predicting force generated by the contralateral than the ipsilateral hand.
source: indicating that the STNr LFP was more informative in predicting force generated by the contralateral than the ipsilateral hand
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical comparisons of prediction accuracy.

claim: The median values of the within-trial correlation coefficients increased with the average movement related synchronisation in the gamma band, with an exponential model explaining 75.7% (p<0.001) of the variance in WithinR.
source: The median values of the within-trial correlation coefficients and stable force correlation coefficients increased with the average movement related synchronisation in the gamma band, with an exponential model y=a*e−bx+k explaining 75.7% (p<0.001) of the variance in WithinR
evidence: This is a quantitative result from regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: An exponential model explained 88.1% (p<0.001) of the variance in StableR across STNs with respect to gamma band synchronization.
source: 88.1% (p<0.001) of the variance in StableR across STNs
evidence: This is a quantitative result from regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The movement-related synchronisation in gamma activity dropped by 71 ± 7.7% from the bipolar channel showing the most movement-related modulation to the average modulation in the remaining two bipolar channels.
source: This assumption was borne out by the fact that the movement-related synchronisation in gamma activity dropped by 71 ± 7.7% from the bipolar channel showing the most movement-related modulation to the average modulation in the remaining two bipolar channels.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data supporting the spatial specificity of gamma activity.

claim: The drop in movement related modulation in the beta band was 59 ± 7.9% from the most modulated channel to the average of remaining channels.
source: This drop was not so acute, 59 ± 7.9%, for movement related modulation in the beta band
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: There was a lack of significant correlation between the accuracy of the prediction of force and baseline beta activity across subjects.
source: Finally, there was a lack of significant correlation between the accuracy of the prediction of force and baseline beta (Spearman r = 0.468, p=0.13 for WithinR; Spearman r = 0.363, p=0.25 for StableR)
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: There was a lack of significant correlation between the accuracy of the prediction of force and baseline gamma activity across subjects.
source: or gamma activity (Spearman r = 0.281, p=0.37 for WithinR; Spearman r = 0.273, p=0.39 for StableR) measured during rest across subjects
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: It is the reactivity of the power changes during gripping that is important for prediction, perhaps because it is more specific for the corresponding motor representation.
source: suggesting that it is the reactivity of the power changes during gripping that is important for prediction, perhaps because it is more specific for the corresponding motor representation
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation with baseline activity.

claim: In the independent patient group performing maximal effort gripping, the median correlation coefficient between predicted force and measured force for individual trials ranged between 0.3848 and 0.9421 for the 20 STNs and contralateral hand.
source: The median correlation coefficient between predicted force and measured force for individual trials (median WithinR) ranged between 0.3848 and 0.9421 for the 20 STNs and contralateral hand (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation study shown in Figure 7.

claim: Considering all 397 individual trials across all STNs in the independent patient group, more than 50% of the trials had WithinR more than 0.7859.
source: Considering all the 397 individual trials across all STNs, more than 50% of the trials had WithinR more than 0.7859 (Figure 7C and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cross-validation study shown in Figure 7.

claim: Incorporating alpha activity (Model 4) improved the force prediction accuracy for maximal effort gripping in the independent patient group.
source: We also found that incorporating alpha activity (Model 4) improved the force prediction accuracy for maximal effort gripping in this patient group.
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-validation analysis.

claim: When Model 4 was used in the independent patient group, more than 50% of all individual trials had WithinR more than 0.8699.
source: When Model 4 was used, the median WithinR ranged between 0.6731 and 0.9625 across all STNs, and more than 50% of all individual trials had WithinR more than 0.8699.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model comparison in the cross-validation study.

claim: BIC analysis showed that Model 4 was significantly better than Model 2 for the patient group performing maximal effort gripping (∆BIC = 243.3±95.9, t(19)=2.5369, p=0.020).
source: BIC analysis showed that Model 4 (BIC = 2116.2±135.7) was significantly better than Model 2 (BIC = 1873.0±110.3) for this patient group performing maximal effort gripping (∆BIC = 243.3±95.9, t(19)=2.5369, p=0.020 comparing the BIC values, Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model comparison shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A large population of STN neurons were modulated by gripping force in patients with Parkinson's disease.
source: This is consistent with an earlier study which recorded neuronal ensemble activities from the STN in patients with Parkinson's disease, and which showed that a large population of STN neurons were modulated by gripping force (Patil et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Frequency-specific LFP activities in the STN correlate with force-related variables in manual grips.
source: This extends the earlier observation that frequency-specific LFP activities in the STN correlate with force-related variables in manual grips (Anzak et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Beta and gamma activities can be considered complementary non-linear correlates of force in gripping, and when combined, afford a measure that linearly correlates with force across all effort levels.
source: and that beta and gamma activities can be considered complementary non-linear correlates of force in gripping, and when combined, afford a measure that linearly correlates with force across all effort levels
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results of the current study.

claim: The first order linear dynamic model proposed here simulates how the musculoskeletal plant responds to the control signal from the brain.
source: the first order linear dynamic model proposed here simulates how the musculoskeletal plant responds to the control signal from the brain
evidence: This is a description of the model's conceptual basis.

claim: The present model describes how the output from the musculoskeletal plant responds to the instantaneous change in the control input from the brain.
source: the present model describes how the output from the musculoskeletal plant, i.e. the generated force, responds to the instantaneous change in the control input from the brain
evidence: This is a description of how the model operates.

claim: The rich information in the gamma band was consistent with prior studies of grasp decoding using ECoG from human motor cortex.
source: The rich information in the gamma band was consistent with prior studies of grasp decoding using ECoG from human motor cortex (Flint et al., 2012, 2014; Pistohl et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Beta desynchronization can encode gripping force, especially at the low effort levels.
source: This is consistent with our previous finding that beta desynchronization can encode gripping force, especially at the low effort levels (Tan et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The predictive power of activities in the beta and gamma band was unlikely to be related to contamination by movement artefacts because bipolar LFPs were used for decoding.
source: It is unlikely that the predictive power of activities in the beta and gamma band was related to contamination by movement artefacts as we used bipolar LFPs for the decoding in which any common artefact is removed through common mode rejection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the recording methodology.

claim: The local motor potential and delta activity (0–4 Hz) in the LFP from the hand area of the primary motor cortex contains information about muscle activity.
source: This contrasts with previous research which showed that the local motor potential and delta activity (0–4 Hz) in the LFP from the hand area of the primary motor cortex contains information about muscle activity (Flint et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Oscillatory activity in the theta/alpha range may be involved in attentional mechanisms.
source: Oscillatory activity in the theta/alpha range may be involved in attentional mechanisms (for review see Palva and Palva, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Alpha activity (7–13 Hz) in the subthalamic nucleus of patients with Parkinson's disease is coherent with parieto-temporal cortical activity in a circuit that has been proposed to subserve attentional functions.
source: In particular, alpha activity (7–13 Hz) in the subthalamic nucleus of patients with Parkinson's disease is coherent with parieto-temporal cortical activity in a circuit that has been proposed to subserve attentional functions (Hirschmann et al., 2011; Litvak et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Reciprocal changes in synchronised oscillatory activity in the STN can potentially provide control signals for the motor plant.
source: Taken as a whole our results suggest that reciprocal changes in synchronised oscillatory activity in the STN can potentially provide control signals for the motor plant.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The motor plant may behave as a first order linear dynamical system translating a basal ganglia effort signal to force for a given effector.
source: We speculate that the motor plant may behave as a first order linear dynamical system translating a basal ganglia effort signal to force for a given effector.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the modeling results.

claim: Changes in the STN LFP preceded changes in the measured force by about 200–300 ms.
source: Note that although the prediction is being used here in terms of its statistical meaning of accounting for the variance in a second signal, it also satisfies the physiological implications of this term in that changes in the STN LFP preceded changes in the measured force by about 200–300 ms.
evidence: This is a temporal observation from the data analysis.

claim: Effort encoding is relatively lateralised in the basal ganglia.
source: Our quantitative approach also allowed us to demonstrate that effort encoding is relatively lateralised in the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the laterality analysis.

claim: Patients with Parkinson's disease have attenuated power modulation in both the beta band and the gamma band during movement initialization when off dopaminergic medication.
source: Patients with Parkinson's disease have been shown to have attenuated power modulation in both the beta band (Doyle et al., 2005; Devos and Defebvre, 2006; Androulidakis et al., 2007; Anzak et al., 2012) and the gamma band (Androulidakis et al., 2007) during movement initialization
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A diminished range of power modulation in the beta and gamma bands during movement may restrict the dynamic range of the coding of force in gripping in Parkinson's disease.
source: Such a diminished range of power modulation in the beta and gamma bands during movement may restrict the dynamic range of the coding of force in gripping in Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This is an inference connecting observed LFP changes to functional impairment.

claim: Untreated PD patients produce normal muscle activation patterns, but muscle activity is not adequately scaled to produce the required force.
source: This is consistent with previous observations that untreated PD patients produce normal muscle activation patterns, but that muscle activity is not adequately scaled to produce the required force (Berardelli et al., 1986; Turner and Desmurget, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PD patients are weaker off dopaminergic medication or DBS.
source: PD patients are weaker off dopaminergic medication or DBS (Corcos et al., 1996; Alberts et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PD patients show an increased probability of selecting slow movement speeds.
source: and that PD patients show an increased probability of selecting slow movement speeds (Mazzoni et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Parkinsonian patients show abnormally high grip forces when asked to lift and hold an object.
source: This will lead to abnormally high grip forces in Parkinsonian patients, as observed when they are asked to lift and hold an object (Fellows et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Increased force scaling can lead to more coarse control of force and difficulty in finely tuning generated force.
source: Increased force scaling can also lead to the more coarse control of force and difficulty in finely tuning generated force.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of altered force scaling.

claim: Abnormally increased gripping force is observed in precision grasping movements in Parkinson's disease.
source: This is consistent with abnormally increased gripping force observed in precision grasping movements in Parkinson's disease (Wenzelburger et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The STN LFP could provide a high-performance control signal for BMI driven neuroprosthetic grasping in paralysed patients.
source: Our findings suggest that the STN LFP could provide a high-performance control signal for BMI driven neuroprosthetic grasping in paralysed patients
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications based on the study's findings.

claim: Deep brain stimulation has now become a relatively safe procedure.
source: leveraging advances in surgery for deep brain stimulation which has now become a relatively safe procedure (Larson, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Activities from STN and GPi correlate with movement parameters such as movement amplitude and speed.
source: Activities from STN and GPi have been shown to correlate with movement parameters such as movement amplitude and speed (Brücke et al., 2012; Joundi et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activities from STN and GPi are modulated by movement intention.
source: and are also modulated by movement intention (Kühn et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Basal ganglia output has been theorized to regulate movement gain in healthy motor control.
source: Basal ganglia output has been theorized to regulate movement gain in healthy motor control, and can contain important information about the motor vigour (Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008; Turner and Desmurget, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Recordings of STN LFP signals have been shown to be stable over months using an implanted amplifier.
source: Recordings of STN LFP signals have been shown to be stable over months using an implanted amplifier (Quinn et al., 2015; Neumann et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: STN LFP signals are similar at re-operation several years later.
source: and the signals are similar at re-operation several years later (Giannicola et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dopamine increases the reactivity of beta and gamma activities around the time of movement.
source: It is also possible that the predictive potential of the STN LFP might be further improved in patients without Parkinson's disease, as dopamine increases the reactivity of beta and gamma activities around the time of movement (Doyle et al., 2005; Androulidakis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some LFP reactivity is retained when movements are imagined rather than actioned.
source: In this regard, it is important to note that some LFP reactivity is retained when movements are imagined rather than actioned (Kühn et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Peripheral afferents may not be necessary for the beta suppression and gamma increases tracked in this study.
source: suggesting that peripheral afferents may not be necessary for the beta suppression and gamma increases tracked here
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about imagined movements.

claim: Microelectrode recordings suggest some spatial segregation in activity related to different limbs in the human STN.
source: although microelectrode recordings suggest some spatial segregation in activity related to different limbs in the human STN (Rodriguez-Oroz et al., 2001; Theodosopoulos et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Plasticity of cortical control signals is likely to play a significant role in the maximisation of the performance of BMIs.
source: Finally, plasticity of cortical control signals is likely to play a significant role in the maximisation of the performance of BMIs (Carmena et al., 2003; Ganguly and Carmena, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Force was unable to be predicted in about half of the patients in the study.
source: First and foremost, we were unable to predict the force in about half of our patients.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged based on the study results.

claim: Seven out of the nine electrodes affording force prediction were on target according to imaging review.
source: According to this standard seven out of the nine electrodes affording force prediction were on target, with the other two electrodes in the posterolateral tail of STN.
evidence: This is based on post-operative imaging review.

claim: Significant movement-related spectral modulation in the beta and gamma bands might be a good electrophysiological marker of proximity to the STN.
source: This suggests that significant movement-related spectral modulation in the beta and gamma bands, -the basis for selecting out this group in the first place, might be a good electrophysiological marker of proximity to the STN
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electrode localization data.

claim: Six out of the 12 electrodes that did not allow reasonable force prediction were identified as neither being in nor touching the STN.
source: In contrast, six out of the 12 electrodes that did not allow reasonable force prediction were identified as neither being in nor touching the STN and these subsequently revised on four sides or left inactive on two sides.
